title: What an operating system is
subtitle: One program that manages every other: it shares the hardware, hides its ugliness, and draws the line between trusted and untrusted code. This chapter builds the whole picture before the later chapters take it apart.

sections.title: The bare machine, and why nobody wants it
sections.body:
Before we study what an operating system does, spend a minute imagining life without one, because that is the only way to feel why it exists, and you will see it is not a pleasant picture at all. Imagine you are handed a computer with nothing installed on it. There is a processor that executes instructions, some memory that holds bytes, a disk that stores blocks of 512 or 4096 bytes, a network card that sends frames, a keyboard that raises a signal when a key goes down. That is all the hardware offers. To print the word “hello” you would have to know which register of which controller chip to write, in what order, with what timing, and then wait politely for the device to say it is done. To store a file you would decide which sectors it occupies and remember that decision yourself. To run two programs you would have to make sure neither overwrites the other’s memory. Early programmers did exactly this, by hand, one program at a time.

An operating system (OS) exists to end that misery. It is a program — the first one to run and the last one to stop — whose job is to stand between every other program and the hardware. Nobody sets out to use an operating system; people use a browser, a compiler, a game. The OS is the thing that makes those programs possible to write at all, because it supplies the vocabulary they speak: files, processes, windows, sockets. When an application asks for “the file called report.txt” it is not asking the disk anything; it is asking the OS, which knows how to turn that sentence into sector numbers.

It helps to keep two descriptions of the OS in your head at once, because every design question in this subject is a tension between them. Seen from above — from the application programmer’s chair — the OS is an extended machine: a cleaner, friendlier, more powerful computer than the real one. Seen from below — from the hardware’s chair — the OS is a resource manager: a referee that hands out the processor, memory and devices to competing programs and makes sure they behave. The first description explains abstractions; the second explains policies. Most of this book is one or the other.

Pause here and ask yourself: how would you print a single word using only the raw hardware? The many steps you imagine are exactly what the OS hides from you.

questions.prompt: A programmer calls fopen("data.csv") without knowing where on the disk the file lives. Which role of the OS makes this possible?

choices.text: The resource-manager role, because the disk is a resource.
The extended-machine role: it hides disk geometry behind the abstraction of a named file.
Neither; the C library does it all.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: The disk is indeed a resource, but the question is about hiding detail from the programmer — that is abstraction, the extended-machine view.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Naming a file and letting the OS find the blocks is abstraction. The resource-manager role would be deciding which program may use the disk first.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: The library only forwards the request. The OS owns the file system and the device.

keynotes: The bare machine offers only a processor, memory, a disk of 512 or 4096-byte blocks, a network card and a keyboard signal.
Printing even one word would need knowing which register of which controller chip to write, in what order, with what timing.
The operating system exists to turn this ugly hardware into something usable.

sections.title: The OS as an extended machine
sections.body:
Look at the OS from the programmer’s side and you will find that its great trick is to replace every ugly thing with a clean idea, one abstraction at a time. Each abstraction the OS offers replaces something ugly with something usable. A file replaces numbered disk blocks: you read bytes at an offset, not sectors on a cylinder. A process replaces “the CPU”: each program believes it has a processor to itself, though the hardware has far fewer processors than programs. An address space replaces physical memory: every process sees a private, contiguous array of bytes starting at zero. A socket replaces a network card: two programs exchange a byte stream without thinking about frames, retransmissions or routes. A window replaces a rectangle of pixels in the frame buffer.

Notice what these abstractions have in common. They are all lies that are useful. The disk is not a tree of folders, the memory is not private, and the CPU is not yours — but behaving as if they were makes programs short, portable and safe. A good abstraction hides exactly the detail that varies between machines. That is why the same C program that calls read() works on an SSD, a spinning disk, a USB stick or a network file system: the abstraction is the same, and the OS (through its drivers) does the translation underneath.

The figure follows one tiny request, read(fd, buffer, 4096), downwards through the layers and back up. Watch how many different pieces of the system each take a turn: the system-call boundary, the file system that maps the file offset to a block, the buffer cache that might already hold it, the driver, the controller, and the physical disk. The application sees none of this; it sees only that the buffer is full when read returns.

Pick one abstraction, say the file, and say what it hides from you. Can you name the ugliness underneath each of the other two?

questions.prompt: Why is it acceptable — even desirable — that the OS “lies” about the hardware?

choices.text: A good lie hides exactly the detail that differs between machines, so programs become simpler and portable.
It is not acceptable; applications should talk to the hardware directly for speed.
Because the lie is actually the truth on every real machine.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The abstraction (file, process, address space) is the contract. Underneath, drivers and the kernel keep the lie consistent.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: Direct access would make every program hardware-specific and unsafe. The tiny speed gain is rarely worth it.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: It is not: real memory is shared, real disks have sectors. The abstraction is deliberately different from the hardware.

figures.caption: Figure 1.2.1 — one read() request, top to bottom
figures.note: Replay it. The application made one call; six components cooperated to answer it.

problems.prompt: List four abstractions an operating system provides, and for each name the hardware detail it hides.
problems.answer: File — disk sectors and their placement. Process — the shared, scarce CPU. Address space — the physical memory layout and other programs’ memory. Socket — frames, retransmission and the network card. (Also acceptable: window — frame-buffer pixels.)

keynotes: A file replaces numbered disk blocks: you read bytes at an offset, not sectors on a cylinder.
A process replaces “the CPU”: each program believes it has a processor to itself.
An address space replaces physical memory: every process sees a private, contiguous array of bytes starting at zero.

sections.title: The OS as a resource manager
sections.body:
Now turn the picture upside down and look from below, where the OS is less a servant and more a referee deciding who gets what. Now look from below. A computer has a handful of expensive, shareable resources: processor time, memory space, disk space, device access, network bandwidth. Several programs, and often several people, want them at once. Someone has to decide who gets what, and when. That someone is the OS, and its job has three parts that always travel together: allocation (hand out the resource), protection (stop one user from damaging another), and accounting (keep track of who used how much, for fairness or billing).

Resources are shared in one of two ways. Some are shared in time — the CPU and the printer are used by one program at a time, taking turns, so the OS’s job is to decide the order and the length of each turn (scheduling). Others are shared in space — memory and disk are divided into pieces and each program gets its own piece at the same moment, so the OS’s job is to carve, track and reclaim the pieces (memory management, file allocation). Almost every OS algorithm you will meet is either a time-sharing policy or a space-sharing policy.

Keep one more idea in mind: mechanism versus policy. A mechanism is how something is done (a timer interrupt that stops a running program every 10 ms); a policy is what is decided (which program runs next). Good systems keep the two separate so the policy can change without rewriting the machinery. When the exam asks you to “compare scheduling algorithms”, you are comparing policies that all run on the same mechanism.

Think of a shared house with one kitchen: which of allocation, protection and accounting is the OS doing when it makes a rota? Notice how the three always travel together.

questions.prompt: Which resource is shared in SPACE rather than in time?

choices.text: The CPU.
A single printer.
Main memory — each process holds its own region at the same moment.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: A CPU core executes one process at a time; processes take turns, so it is shared in time.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: The printer is used by one job at a time — time-sharing again, usually via a spooler.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Memory is divided into pieces and every resident process owns one. The CPU, by contrast, is time-multiplexed.

problems.prompt: A timer interrupt fires every 10 ms and the scheduler picks the process with the shortest remaining time. Identify the mechanism and the policy.
problems.answer: Mechanism: the periodic timer interrupt that regains control from a running process. Policy: “choose the shortest remaining time next” (SRT). Swapping the policy for round robin would not change the mechanism.

keynotes: A computer has a handful of expensive, shareable resources: processor time, memory space, disk space, device access and network bandwidth.
Several programs and users want them at once, and someone has to decide who gets what, and when.
The job has three parts that travel together: allocation, protection and accounting.

sections.title: What the hardware must provide: modes, interrupts, protection
sections.body:
An OS can only enforce rules if the hardware lets it, and you can understand modern computers by asking what features a processor must offer so that a mere program cannot overthrow its own referee. An operating system cannot enforce anything unless the hardware helps. If every instruction could be executed by every program, any program could disable interrupts, overwrite the OS or read your files. So processors provide a small set of features that make an OS possible. The first is the dual mode of operation: a mode bit that is either user or kernel (supervisor). In user mode the CPU refuses privileged instructions — I/O, changing the memory map, halting the machine, disabling interrupts. In kernel mode everything is allowed. Applications run in user mode; only the kernel runs in kernel mode, and the only way into kernel mode is through a controlled entry point (a system call, an interrupt, or a trap).

The second feature is memory protection: base and limit registers (or, in modern CPUs, page tables managed by a memory-management unit) that make each process’s addresses legal only inside its own region. A wild pointer then causes a fault the kernel can handle, instead of silently corrupting a neighbour. The third is the timer: a device that interrupts the CPU after a set interval, guaranteeing the OS regains control even from a program stuck in an infinite loop. Without the timer, a single buggy program could keep the processor forever; with it, preemptive multitasking is possible.

The fourth feature, and the one that makes I/O efficient, is the interrupt: a signal from a device (or from the CPU itself) that makes the processor stop what it is doing, save its place, run a handler and then resume. Instead of the CPU asking the disk every microsecond “are you finished yet?” (polling), the disk taps the CPU on the shoulder when it is. The next sections show the two ways to cross from user into kernel mode: voluntarily (a system call) and involuntarily (an interrupt or exception).

Close your eyes and list the four features in your own words: the mode bit, privileged instructions, memory protection and the timer. Which one stops a program from hogging the CPU for ever?

questions.prompt: A user program executes the instruction that disables all interrupts. What should happen?

choices.text: The CPU raises a protection fault, because that is a privileged instruction; the kernel then typically kills the process.
Interrupts are disabled until the program ends.
Nothing — the instruction is simply ignored with no fault.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Privileged instructions are legal only in kernel mode. Allowing user code to disable interrupts would let it keep the CPU forever.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: That is exactly the danger the mode bit prevents.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: Hardware raises an exception so the OS learns about the violation; silent ignoring would hide bugs and attacks.

figures.caption: Figure 1.4.1 — the two modes
figures.note: The mode bit flips only at a controlled doorway — never by the application’s choice alone.

problems.prompt: Why is a timer interrupt essential for a multi-user OS, even if all the programs are well written?
problems.answer: Without the timer the OS cannot be sure of regaining control: a program that never makes a system call and never blocks would hold the CPU indefinitely. The timer forces a switch back into the kernel at a fixed interval so the scheduler can run another process. Well-written programs can still contain bugs, and users may share a machine with programs they did not write.

keynotes: Dual mode of operation uses a mode bit that is either user or kernel (supervisor).
In user mode the CPU refuses privileged instructions such as I/O and changing the mode.
The hardware must also provide memory protection, a timer and interrupts.

sections.title: System calls: the controlled doorway
sections.body:
A user program is shut out of the kernel by design, so how does it ask for anything? Through one carefully guarded doorway, and you have been walking through it every time you printed or opened a file. A system call is a request from a user program for a service only the kernel may perform. In C you rarely see one directly; you call a library function such as printf, fopen or malloc, and the library, at the right moment, executes a special instruction (syscall, int 0x80, svc) that traps into the kernel. The CPU switches to kernel mode, jumps to a fixed handler address, the kernel validates the arguments, performs the work, and returns with the result — switching back to user mode on the way out.

System calls fall into familiar families. Process control: fork, exec, wait, exit. File management: open, read, write, close, lseek. Device management: ioctl, read/write on device files. Information maintenance: getpid, time. Communication: pipe, socket, send, recv, shared memory. Protection: chmod, chown. Parameters travel in registers (fastest, but limited in number), in a block of memory whose address is passed in a register (Linux uses registers for up to six arguments; larger structures go by pointer), or on the stack.

Crossing the boundary is not free. The CPU must switch modes, save and restore registers, possibly flush parts of the pipeline, and the kernel must check every pointer the user passed (never trust a pointer from user space). A system call costs on the order of a hundred nanoseconds to a microsecond — trivial once, painful a million times. That is why stdio buffers: fputc fills a user-space buffer and only calls write when it is full, turning thousands of calls into one. The worked example below puts numbers on that.

Next time you call printf, picture the journey: library, trap, kernel mode, validation, work, return. Where does the argument checking happen, and why must it?

worked.why: Read a 1 MB file one byte at a time with read(fd, &ch, 1). How many system calls?
Assume each call costs about 0.5 µs of crossing overhead alone.
Now read it in 4 KB blocks.
Overhead falls by a factor of 4096; the crossing cost becomes negligible.

questions.prompt: printf("hi") is a library function, not a system call. Where is the system call?

choices.text: There is none; printf talks to the terminal directly.
Inside the library: after formatting and buffering, it eventually calls write() to send the bytes to the console.
printf is itself a system call.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: User code cannot access the device; the write must go through the kernel.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The library wraps the system call, adding formatting and buffering so applications make far fewer crossings.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: It is a C library function. The kernel offers write(), not printf().

questions.prompt: Why must the kernel validate pointers passed in a system call?

choices.text: A user could pass an address belonging to the kernel or another process, tricking the kernel into reading or overwriting memory the user may not touch.
Pointers are always valid in C.
To make the call faster.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Kernel mode can touch everything, so every argument from user space is untrusted input.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: A pointer is just a number; nothing guarantees it points to legal memory.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: Validation costs time; it is done for safety, not speed.

problems.prompt: A program copies a 2 MB file using a 512-byte buffer (read, then write, per chunk). How many system calls does it make for the copy loop? With a 64 KB buffer?
problems.answer: 2 MB = 2,097,152 bytes. With 512 bytes: 4096 chunks, each needing one read and one write → 8192 calls. With 64 KB: 32 chunks → 64 calls. A 128× larger buffer cuts crossings 128-fold.

keynotes: A system call is a request from a user program for a service only the kernel may perform.
The library executes a special instruction (syscall, int 0x80, svc) that traps into the kernel; the CPU switches to kernel mode and jumps to a fixed handler address.
The kernel validates the arguments, performs the work and returns to the user program.

sections.title: Interrupts, traps and exceptions
sections.body:
The processor normally walks through instructions one after another, and three kinds of event can tap it on the shoulder and send it elsewhere, so it is worth learning how to tell them apart. The CPU normally fetches and executes instructions in order. Three events can divert it. An interrupt is an asynchronous signal from outside the running instruction stream — a disk finished, a packet arrived, the timer expired, a key was pressed. A trap is a deliberate software-generated transfer, such as the system-call instruction. An exception (or fault) is raised by the instruction itself when something is wrong — divide by zero, illegal opcode, a page that is not in memory, an access outside the process’s limits. All three are handled the same way: the hardware saves the program counter and flags, looks up a handler address in the interrupt vector (an array indexed by the interrupt number) and jumps to it in kernel mode.

The handler — the interrupt service routine — does the minimum urgent work (acknowledge the device, copy a byte, wake a sleeping process) and returns. The kernel splits its work into a short top half that runs with interrupts disabled and a longer bottom half (softirq, tasklet, deferred work) that runs later with interrupts enabled, so the system stays responsive. Interrupts have priorities: a higher-priority interrupt may interrupt a lower-priority handler, but not the reverse, and the kernel can mask (temporarily ignore) interrupts in critical sections.

Compare the two ways of waiting for a device. With polling the CPU loops, reading a status register until it says “ready” — simple, and fast if the wait is a few cycles, but it burns the processor for the entire wait. With interrupt-driven I/O the CPU starts the operation, goes off to run another process, and is interrupted when the device finishes. For slow devices (a disk takes milliseconds, enough for millions of instructions) interrupts are enormously better. You will meet a third approach, DMA, in the I/O chapter.

Classify each of these as an interrupt, a trap or an exception: a key press, the system-call instruction, a divide by zero. Which are synchronous and which asynchronous?

worked.why: A disk read takes 8 ms. The CPU runs at 3 × 10⁹ instructions/s (1 instruction per cycle for simplicity). How many instructions could it execute while it waits?

questions.prompt: Which of these is an exception (fault) rather than an interrupt?

choices.text: A process divides an integer by zero.
The network card receives a packet.
The timer expires.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The instruction itself caused the event, so it is synchronous with the program. Interrupts come from devices, independently of the instruction stream.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: That comes from a device asynchronously — an interrupt.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: Also external and asynchronous — an interrupt.

questions.prompt: When is polling actually a sensible choice?

choices.text: For every disk read.
Never — interrupts are always better.
When the expected wait is shorter than the cost of an interrupt, such as a device that responds within a few cycles.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: A disk wait is millions of instructions; polling would waste them all.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: Not always: for very short waits, or at very high interrupt rates, polling is cheaper.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The overhead of saving state and switching can exceed a very short wait; very fast network cards even use polling at high load.

figures.caption: Figure 1.6.1 — servicing an interrupt
figures.note: The interrupted process never notices — its registers are restored exactly.

problems.prompt: A keyboard interrupt handler takes 20 µs and the user types 10 keys per second. What fraction of CPU time does the keyboard handler consume?
problems.answer: 10 interrupts/s × 20 µs = 200 µs of every second = 0.02 % of the CPU — a good reason to prefer interrupts over polling for slow devices.

keynotes: An interrupt is an asynchronous signal from outside the running instruction stream: a disk finished, a packet arrived, the timer expired, a key was pressed.
A trap is a deliberate software-generated transfer, such as the system-call instruction.
An exception (or fault) is raised by the instruction itself when something is wrong, such as divide by zero.

sections.title: How kernels are organised
sections.body:
Everything we have described lives inside the kernel, and the kernel itself is a program that has to be organised somehow, with five classic designs that exams love to compare. Everything above lives inside the kernel. How should that program itself be structured? There are five classic answers, and exam questions love to compare them. A monolithic kernel (traditional Unix, Linux) puts the scheduler, memory manager, file systems, network stack and drivers in one big program sharing one address space. Calls between parts are ordinary function calls, so it is fast; the price is that a bug in any driver can overwrite anything and crash the whole system. Linux softens this with loadable kernel modules: drivers and file systems that can be added to a running kernel without rebooting.

A layered design stacks strict levels — hardware at the bottom, user interface at the top — where each layer uses only the one below. It is easy to verify layer by layer (Dijkstra’s THE system was built this way), but layering is hard to apply cleanly (does the swap-space manager sit above or below the scheduler?) and each extra layer adds overhead. A microkernel (Mach, QNX, MINIX, L4, seL4) keeps in the privileged kernel only the bare minimum — address spaces, scheduling basics and inter-process communication — and runs file systems, drivers and the network stack as ordinary user-mode servers that exchange messages. A crashed driver is just a crashed process that can be restarted, which makes the system dependable and easy to extend; the cost is that every service call turns into messages and context switches.

Real systems are rarely pure. Hybrid kernels (Windows NT, macOS/XNU) keep a microkernel-like structure but run many services in kernel space for speed. Exokernels go to the other extreme: the kernel only multiplexes raw hardware securely and leaves all abstraction to application-linked library operating systems, giving applications maximum control. Finally, virtual machine structures run complete guest operating systems on top of a hypervisor — the subject of the last chapter.

For each design, finish the sentence “it is fast / safe because…”. Which design would you pick for a pocket device, and which for a server?

worked.why: A file read in a microkernel needs 2 messages (request and reply) between the application and the file server, and 2 more between the file server and the disk driver. If each message costs 3 µs and the monolithic version does the same work with plain calls costing 0.4 µs in total, what is the slowdown?

questions.prompt: What is the main price of a microkernel?

choices.text: It cannot run on modern hardware.
It has no memory protection.
More message passing between user-mode servers, so each service call is slower.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: Microkernels such as QNX and seL4 run well on modern hardware.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: Quite the opposite: protection between services is its selling point.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Isolation is bought with context switches and copies: a file read becomes a message to the file server and a reply.

questions.prompt: What do Linux loadable kernel modules give a monolithic kernel?

choices.text: They move drivers out to user mode for safety.
The ability to add or remove drivers and file systems at run time without rebooting, while still running in kernel mode.
They make the kernel layered.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: Modules run in kernel mode with full privilege; that is the risk.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: It keeps monolithic speed but adds some of the extensibility of a microkernel — though a faulty module can still crash the kernel.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: Modules are unrelated to layering.

questions.prompt: Why are Windows NT and macOS called hybrid kernels?

choices.text: They run on two kinds of processor.
They are written half in C and half in assembly.
They have a microkernel-like design but run many services in kernel space for performance.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: Hybrid refers to kernel structure, not hardware.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: Language mix is not what “hybrid” means here.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: It is a compromise between the isolation of a microkernel and the speed of a monolithic kernel.

figures.caption: Figure 1.7.1 — two kernel designs
figures.note: Where the privilege boundary sits decides speed versus isolation.
figures.script:
diagram("direction: right
group "Monolithic" { m1, m2 }
group "Microkernel" { u1, u2, mk }
[Everything in one privileged kernel] as m1 #violet
[Hardware] as m2 #grey
[File server (user mode)] as u1 #blue
[Driver (user mode)] as u2 #blue
[Tiny kernel: IPC, scheduling, memory] as mk #violet
m1 -> m2 : function calls
u1 -> mk : message
u2 -> mk : message");

problems.prompt: Compare monolithic and microkernel designs on (a) speed, (b) reliability, (c) extensibility.
problems.answer: Speed: monolithic faster (function calls, no message copies); microkernel slower. Reliability: microkernel better — a failing driver or file server is an isolated user process that can be restarted; in a monolithic kernel it can corrupt everything. Extensibility: microkernel easier — add a server without touching the kernel; monolithic needs modules or a rebuild.

keynotes: A monolithic kernel (traditional Unix, Linux) puts the scheduler, memory manager, file systems, network stack and drivers in one program sharing one address space.
Calls between its parts are ordinary function calls, so it is fast, but a bug in any driver can crash everything.
Other classic designs are layered, microkernel, modular and hybrid, which trade speed against safety and flexibility.

sections.title: From power button to login prompt
sections.body:
When you press the power button there is no OS anywhere in memory, so how does the machine pull itself up by its own bootstraps? Follow the chain and you will see. At power-on there is no OS in memory, only firmware in non-volatile storage. The CPU starts executing at a fixed address and runs the firmware, which tests the hardware (POST), finds a boot device and loads a first program. Legacy BIOS reads the first 512-byte sector of the disk — the MBR — into memory and jumps to it. Those 512 bytes contain 446 bytes of boot code, a 64-byte partition table (four entries of 16 bytes) and a 2-byte signature (0x55AA). The code is far too small to load a kernel from a file system, so it merely loads a bigger bootloader (GRUB, LILO, the Windows Boot Manager) that does understand file systems.

Modern machines use UEFI: firmware that itself understands the FAT file system, reads a bootloader from an EFI system partition on a GPT disk, and can verify the bootloader’s digital signature (secure boot) so malware cannot slip in before the OS. Either way, the bootloader locates the kernel image, loads it into memory (together with an initial RAM disk containing the drivers needed to reach the real root file system), and jumps to it. The kernel then initialises memory management, the scheduler and devices, mounts the root file system, and starts the first user process — init or systemd on Linux — which in turn starts every service and finally the login prompt or the graphical shell.

The pattern to remember is bootstrapping: each stage is small and simple and is just capable enough to load the next, larger stage. That is why the sector is so tiny, why the bootloader is separate from the kernel, and why an OS can be updated by replacing files without touching the firmware.

Say the sequence aloud: firmware, POST, boot device, first sector, boot loader, kernel, login. Which step is the first to run code you could replace?

worked.why: Firmware reads sector 0 (512 bytes). How is it laid out?
The partition table holds 4 entries; each entry is therefore how big?

questions.prompt: Why is the MBR bootloader so small?

choices.text: To save disk space.
It must fit in one 512-byte sector the firmware can read before any file system exists.
Because the kernel is tiny.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: One sector is nothing on a modern disk; the limit comes from what firmware loads, not from capacity.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The firmware knows nothing about files; it can only read sector 0. That tiny code loads a bigger loader that does understand file systems.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: Kernels are megabytes; the MBR code only starts the chain.

questions.prompt: What does UEFI secure boot add over BIOS?

choices.text: It makes the machine boot faster.
It verifies a digital signature on the bootloader (and kernel) so unsigned or tampered code is refused.
It encrypts the whole disk.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: Speed is not its purpose; verification costs a little time.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The chain of trust starts in firmware, blocking boot-time malware.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: Disk encryption is a separate feature.

figures.caption: Figure 1.8.1 — the boot chain
figures.note: Each stage is small and loads the next, bigger one.

problems.prompt: List, in order, the stages from power-on to the login prompt and name what each one loads.
problems.answer: 1) Firmware (BIOS/UEFI) runs POST and loads the first-stage loader from the boot device. 2) Bootloader (e.g. GRUB) loads the kernel image and initrd. 3) Kernel initialises devices and memory, mounts the root file system. 4) init/systemd starts services. 5) Login prompt or display manager.

keynotes: At power-on only firmware in non-volatile storage exists; the CPU starts at a fixed address and runs it to test the hardware (POST).
Legacy BIOS reads the first 512-byte sector of the disk, the MBR, into memory and jumps to it.
Those 512 bytes hold 446 bytes of boot code and a 64-byte partition table of four 16-byte entries.

sections.title: How we got here: a short history of operating systems
sections.body:
Every feature of a modern OS was invented to cure a particular pain, and if you follow the pains in order the history reads like a detective story. The features of a modern OS were each invented to cure a particular pain. The first computers had no OS: a programmer booked the machine, loaded a program by hand and watched it run. Setting up took longer than running, and the expensive CPU sat idle. Batch systems fixed the set-up cost: operators grouped similar jobs on cards or tape and a small resident monitor loaded them one after another. But a job waiting for the card reader or tape still left the CPU idle, because I/O devices were thousands of times slower than the processor.

The cure was multiprogramming: keep several jobs in memory at once, and when one waits for I/O let another use the CPU. This single idea creates almost everything in this course — memory management (several jobs must fit), CPU scheduling (which job next?), protection (jobs must not interfere), and synchronisation. Time-sharing extended it by switching so quickly (every few milliseconds) that many users at terminals each felt they had the machine to themselves; this brought interactive response, virtual memory and file systems with access control (CTSS, MULTICS, then UNIX). Personal computers returned to one user per machine but kept the ideas; distributed and cloud systems spread the same ideas over many machines; mobile and embedded systems added tight limits on power and memory; real-time systems added deadlines.

The derivation below turns the multiprogramming argument into a number — it is one of the most quoted results in the subject because it shows why an OS keeps several programs in memory.

For each era, batch, multiprogramming, time sharing, personal computers, name the pain it cured. Seeing the cause makes the feature easy to remember.

derivation.why: Suppose each process spends a fraction p of its time waiting for I/O (so it needs the CPU a fraction 1 − p of its time). With only one process in memory, the CPU is busy just 1 − p of the time.

With n independent processes in memory, the CPU is idle only when all of them are waiting at the same moment. If the waits are independent, the probability they are all waiting is the product of their individual probabilities.
The CPU is busy whenever at least one process is ready, which is the complement.

The model is optimistic — it assumes independence and ignores context-switch overhead — but it explains the trend: more resident processes drive utilisation toward 100 %, with diminishing returns once p^n is small. The degree of multiprogramming n is limited by memory, which is why memory management matters.

worked.why: Each process waits for I/O 80 % of the time (p = 0.8). Utilisation with 4 processes in memory?
Adding a fifth process raises it to 1 − 0.8⁵ = 67.2 %, a gain of about 8 percentage points. Whether that extra process is worth its memory is a policy decision.

choices.text: Users waiting in a queue to use the card reader.
Programs being too large for the computer.
The CPU sitting idle while one job waited for slow I/O.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: That motivated batch processing and spooling, not multiprogramming itself.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: That is a memory-management problem (overlays, virtual memory).

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Keeping several jobs in memory lets the CPU run another when one blocks.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes time-sharing from plain multiprogramming?

choices.text: It switches among jobs so frequently that each interactive user perceives a fast, dedicated response.
It uses more than one CPU.
It has no memory protection.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Multiprogramming switches mainly on I/O waits; time-sharing adds a timer-driven rotation for interactivity.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: Time-sharing was invented on single-CPU machines.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: Protection was essential for it.

figures.caption: Figure 1.9.1 — CPU utilisation = 1 − pⁿ
figures.note: Each column adds one more process in memory. The 80 % row is the one to study: a single process leaves the CPU 80 % idle; ten of them keep it ~89 % busy.

problems.prompt: Processes spend 90 % of their time waiting for I/O. What utilisation does 1, 5 and 10 resident processes give, using 1 − pⁿ?
problems.answer: p = 0.9. n = 1: 10 %. n = 5: 1 − 0.59049 = 41.0 %. n = 10: 1 − 0.34868 = 65.1 %. I/O-heavy workloads need many resident processes to keep the CPU busy.

problems.prompt: Using the same model, how many processes are needed (at least) to reach 90 % utilisation when p = 0.8?

keynotes: The first computers had no OS: a programmer booked the machine, loaded a program by hand and watched it run.
Batch systems grouped similar jobs and a small resident monitor loaded them one after another, removing the set-up cost.
Each later step, multiprogramming and time sharing, cured idle time or poor interactivity.

sections.title: Services an operating system offers
sections.body:
Let’s pull the threads together, because examiners love to ask what an OS actually offers, and you can answer from what you have already learned. Pulling the threads together, a general-purpose OS offers a standard list of services, and examiners like asking for them. For the user and the programmer: a user interface (command line, graphical or touch); program execution (load a program, run it, end it normally or abnormally); I/O operations (programs may not touch devices directly, so the OS performs I/O on their behalf); file-system manipulation (create, delete, read, write, search, manage permissions); communication (processes on one machine or across a network exchange data, through shared memory or message passing); and error detection (hardware faults, device failures, bad programs).

For the system’s own sake the OS also provides resource allocation (CPU cycles, memory, files and devices to many users at once), accounting (who used what) and protection and security (controlling access to resources and defending against outsiders). These are not independent: protecting a file needs the file system; allocating memory needs the hardware’s protection registers; communication needs both. Notice also that the OS is itself a program that must be efficient — time spent running the OS is time not spent running your work, so every service has a cost that the designers constantly trade against its benefit.

Group the services into those for the user and programmer and those for the system itself. Can you explain each with an example from your own laptop?

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT normally an OS service?

choices.text: Program execution.
Compiling source code into an executable.
File-system manipulation.
Error detection.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: Loading and running programs is a core OS service.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: A compiler is an application (system software) that uses the OS, not part of the OS services list.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: Core service.

responses.title: A common shortcut.
responses.body: Core service.

problems.prompt: Which OS service is being used when you copy a file from one folder to another, and which when two programs exchange data through a pipe?
problems.answer: Copying uses file-system manipulation (and I/O operations underneath). The pipe is communication between processes (message passing through the kernel).

keynotes: For users and programmers the OS offers a user interface, program execution, I/O operations and file-system manipulation.
Other services are communication, error detection, resource allocation, accounting and protection and security.
Programs may not touch devices directly, so the OS performs I/O on their behalf.

sections.title: Summary and what comes next
sections.body:
Here is the chapter in a few lines, so you can check what has stuck.

  • An OS is an extended machine (clean abstractions: file, process, address space, socket) and a resource manager (allocation, protection, accounting, sharing in time and space).
  • Hardware makes it possible: dual mode, privileged instructions, memory protection, a timer and interrupts.
  • User code enters the kernel only through system calls, interrupts and exceptions; each crossing has a cost, so libraries buffer.
  • Kernel designs trade speed against isolation: monolithic, layered, microkernel, hybrid, exokernel, virtual machine.
  • Booting is a chain of ever-larger loaders: firmware → bootloader → kernel → init.
  • Multiprogramming (utilisation = 1 − pⁿ) is the idea that created CPU scheduling, memory management and synchronisation.

Next, Chapter 2 opens the first abstraction: the process — what it is, how the OS represents it, and how the scheduler shares the CPU among many of them.

Cover the summary and try to rebuild it from memory. Then look at the bullets you missed and reread those sections.

problems.prompt: In five lines, explain to a friend what an operating system does and why it needs hardware support.
problems.answer: It hides the hardware behind files, processes and memory (extended machine) and decides who uses the CPU, memory and devices (resource manager). It needs a user/kernel mode bit and privileged instructions so programs cannot misuse devices, memory-protection hardware so they cannot overwrite each other, a timer so it can always regain the CPU, and interrupts so devices can signal it without being polled.

keynotes: An OS is an extended machine (file, process, address space, socket) and a resource manager (allocation, protection, accounting, sharing in time and space).
Hardware makes it possible with dual mode, privileged instructions, memory protection, a timer and interrupts.
User code enters the kernel only through system calls, interrupts and exceptions, and each crossing has a cost.
